Reinforcement learning for optical impairment correction

A bandit proof of concept that identified useful equalizer coefficients in roughly 1,000 rounds, motivating a scalable Q-learning formulation.

Case study

Turn equalizer search into sequential decision-making.

UCBQ-learningPMDAdaptive filters

The problem

A 2×2 polarization equalizer already contains many coupled complex coefficients. Even a heavily discretized toy version produces 3¹²—more than 531,000—possible filter combinations, which makes exhaustive evaluation impractical.

Bandit proof of concept

The first formulation treats coefficient sets as arms and negative CMA error as the reward. UCB balances exploration and exploitation, finding the strongest tested set in roughly 1,000 rounds for the compact case.

Scaling with Q-learning

Rather than selecting a complete filter independently each time, the Q-learning state represents the current coefficients and actions increment, decrement, or keep individual elements. This reduces the decision to 72 local actions and makes experience replay or a deep Q-network natural next steps.

Takeaway

The project clarifies where reinforcement learning helps—and where a naive action space breaks down. The useful shift is from choosing among every possible equalizer to learning how to navigate the coefficient space.
